title: The Amazing History of Soda
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of soda, starting with mineral water's supposed health benefits in Europe and the early attempts to artificially carbonate water: Joseph Priestley's 1767 experiment, Johann Jakob Schweppe's compression pump and company, Charles Plinth's soda siphon, and John Matthews' lead-chamber carbon dioxide generator. They cover Benjamin Silliman's failed soda fountains in New York, the rise of soda fountains tied to pharmacies, soda jerks, small beer and root beer origins, drugs (including cocaine) in early sodas and phosphates, and John Pemberton's Coca-Cola, with its disputed cocaine content. They also discuss flavored sodas, the soda fountain's link to bars and Prohibition and temperance, its decline after the mid-twentieth century due to car culture and the bottle cap, and close with listener mail from a teacher who changed careers after the show's advice.

segments.title: Opening banter and soda fountain nostalgia
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of soda and soda fountains, joke about 1950s nostalgia and Happy Days, and note that soda fountains were already declining by the forties and fifties. They mention a Dorito Effect book recommendation and that Pellegrino is artificially carbonated.

segments.title: Mineral water and early carbonation experiments
segments.summary: Mineral water was believed to have healing powers in Europe. Joseph Priestley in 1767 made a crude carbonated drink using yeast mash. Johann Jakob Schweppe later built a hand-crank compression pump and found cold temperatures and pressure aid carbonation. Carbon dioxide was made with sulfuric acid and powdered marble.

segments.title: Soda siphon and John Matthews' generator
segments.summary: Charles Plinth perfected the soda siphon, which still needed a constant source of carbon dioxide. John Matthews then developed a lead-chamber apparatus that generated carbon dioxide and could serve many drinks, but it was immobile, so drinks were made on site, leading to the soda fountain.

segments.title: Stamps.com sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Stamps.com offering online postage with an offer code.

segments.title: Benjamin Silliman's failed soda fountains
segments.summary: Yale chemistry professor Benjamin Silliman built two soda fountains in New York City, at the City Hotel and the Tontine Coffee House, using Matthews' design. He served the drink as medicine with no socializing, and his business failed, though competitors later succeeded.

segments.title: Pharmacies, soda jerks, and root beer origins
segments.summary: Soda fountains spread through cities and were run by pharmacists who had the skill to make carbon dioxide safely. Soda jerks, sometimes called soda throwers, were skilled showmen, some former bartenders during Prohibition. Root beer and ginger beer descend from folk small beers used to purify water.

segments.title: Drugs in early sodas, phosphates, and cocaine
segments.summary: Pharmacies added alcohol and drugs such as heroin, morphine, opium, cannabis and cocaine to drinks, which were seen as medicine. The Food and Drug Act of 1906 was a turning point. Phosphate drinks with acid phosphate were popular soda fountain drinks. Quantities of cocaine in drinks are disputed.

segments.title: Coca-Cola origins and the cocaine question
segments.summary: John Pemberton, a Confederate Civil War veteran and pharmacist, created Coca-Cola in the 1880s, sold at Jacob's Pharmacy in Atlanta for a nickel, as a solution for soldiers addicted to narcotics. Frank Robinson named it and designed the script. The drink's cocaine content is debated, with Coca-Cola saying none was included. Seven Up also once contained lithium citrate.

segments.title: Flavors, temperance, Prohibition, and decline of soda fountains
segments.summary: Early flavors included citrus, cherry, vanilla, wintergreen, and grape. Soda fountains competed with bars, and during the temperance movement they were promoted as alternatives; Ray Catherine May argues Prohibition helped soda shops. Soda fountains declined due to car culture and the bottle cap. Hosts mention the World of Coke in Atlanta.

segments.title: Listener mail: career change to teaching
segments.summary: A listener named Catherine, now Mrs. Young, thanks the hosts for advice to do what you love, which helped her move into teaching, and says she will start teaching Year 6 in the UK.
